meta.tier_interpretation_note: These tiers reflect April reservoir storage levels relative to percentile thresholds (50th/33rd/20th percentiles as described, based on recent historical CDEC-available data as of July 2025). Laws rarely set storage-percentile targets; they influence storage by constraining releases (environmental flows, water quality/temperature, downstream water rights, Delta water quality), limiting exports, requiring flood-control space, and shaping operating rules during drought. Likelihood scores reflect policy-to-outcome plausibility (how directly a legal standard can drive storage conditions toward that tier), not a guarantee of achieving any tier.

Legal Standards.name: Flood control requirements and operating rules (e.g., flood-control space requirements in reservoir rule curves / water control manuals)
Legal Standards.note: Many major reservoirs must maintain flood-control space during wet periods, which can require releases that reduce storage—even when inflows are high. These operational constraints can strongly shape April storage levels, often limiting how ‘full’ a reservoir can be at a given time.

key_elements.plain_definition: An operating target that sets how much storage must be kept empty (or can be filled) by date to manage flood risk.
The portion of a reservoir intentionally kept empty to capture flood inflows.
The official operating document that prescribes how a flood-control reservoir is operated under different conditions.

Legal Standards.name: California water right permits/licenses and SWRCB conditions (including bypass flows, seasonal release terms, and priority/availability limits)
Legal Standards.note: Water right permits/licenses can require bypass flows, limit storage/diversion timing, and constrain releases to protect instream uses and downstream senior rights. In shortages, priority/availability limits and curtailment logic can change what water can be stored or diverted into storage (project- and right-specific).

key_elements.plain_definition: A required amount of water that must remain in the river (not stored/diverted) to protect downstream/instream uses.
Water rights order (senior before junior) that affects who must reduce use first when supplies are short.
An enforceable operating requirement attached to a water right authorization.

Legal Standards.name: Federal Endangered Species Act (ESA) — operational constraints (Section 7 consultation / BiOps / RPAs)
Legal Standards.note: ESA can require operational measures (flows, temperature management, ramping, fish passage/entrainment limits) that change reservoir release patterns. This often reduces stored water availability for other purposes or changes seasonal storage trajectories, depending on hydrology and species needs.

key_elements.plain_definition: Document stating whether a federal action would jeopardize listed species and what conditions are required.
Required operational/habitat changes to avoid jeopardy while allowing the action to proceed.
Unintended harm to listed species allowed only if specified limits and measures are followed.

Legal Standards.name: Central Valley Project Improvement Act (CVPIA) (1992) — fish and wildlife operational/restoration requirements tied to CVP
Legal Standards.note: CVPIA directs fish-and-wildlife-oriented operational actions for the Central Valley Project (CVP), including dedicating and managing water for restoration purposes. These requirements can constrain reservoir operations and reduce storage retained for delivery, particularly in dry years.

key_elements.plain_definition: Water reserved/managed for environmental restoration or protection rather than consumptive delivery.

Legal Standards.name: Clean Water Act + Porter-Cologne (water quality standards/objectives, including temperature and aquatic habitat protections)
Legal Standards.note: Water quality objectives (especially temperature for cold-water fisheries) can require cold-water pool management and minimum releases. These constraints can reduce end-of-winter/early-spring carryover storage or limit refill strategies if releases are needed to meet water quality standards.

key_elements.plain_definition: A numeric/narrative target (e.g., temperature) intended to protect beneficial uses like fish habitat.
The colder, deeper reservoir water needed to meet downstream temperature targets for fish.
Legally protected uses of water (including ecosystem uses like cold freshwater habitat).

Legal Standards.name: Bay-Delta Water Quality Control Plan + D-1641 (Delta outflow/salinity and related operations constraints affecting upstream storage decisions)
Legal Standards.note: Delta water quality/outflow requirements can compel upstream releases and constrain exports, shaping how reservoirs are operated seasonally and how much carryover storage is retained going into spring. While not a ‘storage law,’ it can be a strong driver of release patterns that affect April storage levels.

key_elements.plain_definition: Freshwater flow from the Delta to the Bay; higher outflow often requires upstream releases.
A target limiting how salty the Delta can get, sometimes requiring releases/outflow.

Legal Standards.name: Federal Power Act hydropower licensing (FERC) — minimum flow/ramping/fish passage conditions
Legal Standards.note: Hydropower licenses can impose minimum flows, ramping rate limits, and fish passage/habitat measures that affect dam operations and storage trajectories. Strong leverage for facilities where hydropower license conditions are binding.

key_elements.plain_definition: Limits on how quickly releases can increase or decrease, to reduce harm to fish and habitat.
A required baseline release to protect downstream ecosystems.

Legal Standards.name: CEQA (state) and NEPA (federal) environmental review (procedural requirements affecting storage-related projects and operating changes)
Legal Standards.note: Procedural statutes that can shape reservoir operations indirectly by conditioning approvals for re-operation plans, new infrastructure, forecast-informed operations, spillway changes, and environmental mitigation. They rarely impose day-to-day storage targets, but they can enable or constrain operational flexibility over time.

key_elements.plain_definition: Feasible measures required to reduce significant environmental impacts of a project or operating change.
Evaluation of other approaches that meet the purpose with fewer environmental impacts.

Legal Standards.name: California Dam Safety oversight (operational restrictions tied to dam safety and infrastructure condition)
Legal Standards.note: Dam safety requirements can impose temporary storage caps, release constraints, or operational restrictions if structural issues are present. This can significantly reduce storage in affected reservoirs (highly contingent and site-specific).

key_elements.plain_definition: A mandated cap on how full a reservoir can be (often temporary) for safety reasons.
A limitation on how much water can be safely released, affecting ability to manage floods/refill.

Tier 1.threshold: April storage ≥ top threshold (50th percentile as of July 2025, per reservoir) for ≥90% of years

policies.policy_name: Flood control requirements and rule curves
policies.relationship: Often constrains achieving very high storage frequency (can force lower storage for flood space)
policies.note: Mechanism: Flood-control space requirements commonly prevent reservoirs from staying ‘too full’ by spring in many years, making Tier 1 (very high storage in ≥90% of years) difficult unless hydrology and rule curves allow refill by April.

policies.relationship: More commonly reduces operational flexibility / increases releases than boosts storage
policies.note: Mechanism: ESA often requires releases or operational changes for species protection; it is rarely a direct driver of consistently high April storage across many years.

policies.relationship: Typically a constraint on retaining storage (can require releases/outflow); not a Tier 1 ‘builder’
policies.note: Mechanism: Outflow/salinity obligations can require upstream releases that reduce end-of-winter carryover storage; consistent Tier 1 outcomes require abundant inflow or operational innovations beyond the legal baseline.

Tier 2.threshold: April storage ≥ middle threshold (33rd percentile as of July 2025, per reservoir) for ≥67% of years

policies.policy_name: Flood control requirements and rule curves
policies.relationship: Directly shapes the feasible refill level by April; can be compatible with Tier 2 more often than Tier 1
policies.note: Mechanism: Rule curves determine how much refill is allowed by spring. Tier 2 is plausible where flood-control space can be refilled by April in many years while still meeting downstream safety requirements.

policies.policy_name: Water right permit/license conditions (bypass flows, seasonal terms)
policies.relationship: Direct but basin/project-specific influence on refill and required releases
policies.note: Mechanism: Bypass flow and release terms can reduce refill or require releases; Tier 2 outcomes depend on how stringent conditions are relative to inflows and competing demands.

policies.relationship: Conditional constraint—can require releases that reduce storage but may be managed to maintain moderate storage
policies.note: Mechanism: Temperature objectives can drive cold-water pool management and sometimes winter/spring releases. With careful planning and adequate inflow, Tier 2 storage frequency can still be achievable.

Tier 3.threshold: April storage ≥ middle threshold (33rd percentile as of July 2025, per reservoir) for ≥30% of years

policies.relationship: Often a meaningful driver of release patterns that can pull storage down into Tier 3 ranges (especially in drier years)
policies.note: Mechanism: ESA-driven flow/temperature/entrainment constraints can require releases and reduce retained storage, making Tier 3-level performance (meeting moderate threshold in fewer years) more plausible under stressed hydrology.

policies.relationship: Direct operational constraint that can lower April storage by requiring outflow/salinity-related releases
policies.note: Mechanism: Delta water quality/outflow obligations can drive release patterns that reduce upstream storage, particularly when inflow is limited and obligations remain binding.

policies.relationship: Conditional but potentially strong constraint on storage retained for deliveries in CVP system reservoirs
policies.note: Mechanism: CVPIA fish-and-wildlife operational requirements can reduce the water retained for other purposes and influence carryover, contributing to Tier 3-level storage frequency in some years.

policies.relationship: Direct for affected facilities; can increase required releases and reduce storage
policies.note: Mechanism: Minimum flow and ramping constraints can require releases that reduce storage, especially if not aligned with water supply conditions.

Tier 4.threshold: Reservoir storage below the middle threshold (at or below the lower threshold = 20th percentile as of July 2025) for >70% of years (April values); i.e., not meeting Tier 1–3 conditions

policies.policy_name: Flood control requirements and rule curves (plus extreme hydrology)
policies.relationship: Can contribute to persistently low April storage if rule curves are conservative and refill is limited (but hydrology is often the dominant driver)
policies.note: Mechanism: Conservative flood rules can limit refill; however, Tier 4 typically reflects sustained low inflows/drought and/or high obligatory releases that prevent carryover.

policies.policy_name: ESA + Bay-Delta Plan/D-1641 combined operational constraints
policies.relationship: Combined constraints can strongly reduce storage flexibility in dry years; can help explain persistent low storage frequency when obligations remain binding
policies.note: Mechanism: When ESA measures and Delta outflow/water quality obligations require releases during drought, reservoirs may fail to refill in most years, pushing outcomes toward Tier 4.

policies.relationship: Highly contingent but can be a strong driver of very low storage where restrictions exist
policies.note: Mechanism: If safety-related caps are imposed, reservoirs can be forced to operate well below normal storage for extended periods—producing Tier 4 behavior for that reservoir regardless of other objectives.

policies.relationship: Indirect—can slow or reshape projects intended to improve storage performance (e.g., forecast-informed operations, spillway/outlet changes, re-operation plans)
policies.note: Mechanism: Environmental review can delay or modify operational changes that might improve refill/carryover; it rarely explains Tier 4 outcomes by itself.

Governing Agencies.name: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE)
Governing Agencies.note: Develops/approves flood-control operating manuals and flood-control space requirements for many reservoirs; influences rule curves and operational constraints that directly affect storage trajectories.

Governing Agencies.name: Reservoir owner/operators (e.g., U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, California Department of Water Resources, local irrigation districts, utilities)
Governing Agencies.note: Operate reservoirs day-to-day within legal constraints (flood rules, water rights terms, environmental requirements, hydropower licenses); operational choices directly shape April storage outcomes subject to hydrology.

Governing Agencies.name: State Water Resources Control Board (SWRCB)
Governing Agencies.note: Administers water rights and can impose permit/license terms (including bypass flows) and implement Bay-Delta Plan requirements through orders/decisions (e.g., D-1641 in Delta operations contexts); also sets water quality objectives under Porter-Cologne via statewide/regional planning.

Governing Agencies.name: Regional Water Quality Control Boards (RWQCBs)
Governing Agencies.note: Adopt Basin Plans and enforce water quality objectives (including aquatic habitat/temperature-related requirements) that can influence reservoir release patterns and cold-water pool management.

Governing Agencies.name: NOAA Fisheries (NMFS)
Governing Agencies.note: Leads ESA Section 7 consultations for listed anadromous species and issues BiOps/RPAs that can require operational measures affecting reservoir releases and storage.

Governing Agencies.name: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service (USFWS)
Governing Agencies.note: Participates in ESA consultations for species under its jurisdiction and can shape operational measures that affect reservoir releases and storage where relevant.

Governing Agencies.name: U.S. Bureau of Reclamation (USBR)
Governing Agencies.note: Operates CVP reservoirs and implements CVPIA-related operational/restoration requirements; CVP operating decisions strongly affect storage and carryover.

Governing Agencies.name: Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC)
Governing Agencies.note: Licenses hydropower projects and enforces license conditions (minimum flows, ramping, passage measures) that can affect storage and release patterns at hydropower dams.

Governing Agencies.name: California Division of Safety of Dams (DSOD) (within California Department of Water Resources)
Governing Agencies.note: Oversees dam safety and can require operational changes or storage restrictions for safety reasons, which can directly cap storage in affected reservoirs.

Governing Agencies.name: Lead agencies under CEQA / federal action agencies under NEPA
Governing Agencies.note: Conduct environmental review and impose mitigation/conditions for reservoir projects or major operational changes, indirectly shaping storage-related infrastructure and re-operation options over time.
